column1: # Wallpaper catalog used by the installer.
# Fields: file, title, place, time zone, note, fact, light.
# Keep the captions and place facts short and checkable.

column5: note
column6: fact

column5: Sandstone walls worn into waves, lit from a slot far overhead.
column6: Arizona is one of the few places in the United States that does not change its clocks, so for half the year it reads the same as California and for the other half the same as Colorado.

column5: Brick temples standing out of the morning haze across the plain.
column6: Myanmar keeps its clocks half an hour off the hour, which only a handful of countries do.

column5: Dead camelthorn trees on a white clay pan, red dunes behind them.
column6: The trees have been dead for roughly nine hundred years and are still standing. It is too dry there for them to rot.

column5: The cone across a lake, snow still on the upper third.
column6: It is an active volcano. The last eruption was in 1707 and ash reached Tokyo, a hundred kilometres away.

column5: Sharp peaks straight out of the sea, with the water going green in the shallows.
column6: It sits above the Arctic Circle, so from late May to mid July the sun does not set at all.

column5: Cliffs dropping into dark water, cloud caught halfway down.
column6: It is one of the wettest inhabited places on earth, and it is not a sound. A sound is carved by a river and this was carved by a glacier, which makes it a fiord.

column5: A lake of an improbable blue under bare grey peaks.
column6: The colour is rock ground to flour by the glaciers above it. The powder hangs in the water and scatters the blue back out.

column5: Water stepping down through sixteen lakes, turquoise between the trees.
column6: The barriers holding the lakes apart are still being built. Moss and algae lay down limestone as the water runs over them, so the shape of the place changes over a lifetime.

column5: Green ridges under low cloud, the sea somewhere behind.
column6: The Cuillin ridge is gabbro, which is rough enough to climb in bare hands and magnetic enough to send a compass wrong.

column5: Three granite towers over a pale lake, in hard clear light.
column6: The wind off the Southern Patagonian Ice Field regularly passes a hundred kilometres an hour and has been known to knock walkers over.

column5: Three limestone blocks standing alone above the scree.
column6: The front line ran through here in the First World War, and there are tunnels cut through the rock by soldiers who fought at three thousand metres.

column5: A black sand beach with a many-peaked mountain rising straight off it.
column6: Iceland keeps the same time all year and never changes its clocks, which puts sunrise in midsummer at about three in the morning.

column5: Sandstone pillars going up out of the forest, tops lost in mist.
column6: The whole of China runs on one clock, so in the far west the sun can come up at ten in the morning.

column5: Sand, shallow water and nothing else in the frame.
A track going in under a closed canopy.
Close on frozen blades, everything else out of focus.

column2: One tree in an open field
column5: A single tree with room around it and a plain sky behind.
Long grass and flowers, the light low and warm.
Water sitting on green leaves, close enough to see it hold.
Reeds standing in still water with the far bank soft behind them.
A river running out of frame between two slopes.
Snow held on dark branches, the air full of it.
Shallow water breaking over rounded stones.
The water along the shoreline lit blue from inside it.
column6: The light is made by single-celled plankton that flash when the water around them moves, so the glow follows the waves and your own footprints.

column2: A dust storm crossing the dunes
column5: A wall of dust moving across a dune field.
The inside of a glacier, the ice blue where it is thickest.
column6: The caves are made each winter by meltwater draining through the ice, and most of them are gone by spring. They are never the same twice.

column5: Fresh lava crossing dark rock, glowing along the cracks.
column6: Hawaii does not change its clocks either, so for half the year it is two hours behind California and for the other half it is three.

column5: A storm cloud built up over flat country, rain visible under it.
A snow plateau under a low moon, wind carved ridges running to the horizon.
column6: It is the largest high mountain plateau in Europe, and Europe's last big herd of wild reindeer crosses it.

column5: The Milky Way standing over a dry salt basin, mountains low on the horizon.
column6: Parts of it have gone decades without measurable rain, which is why the largest telescopes on earth are built there.

column5: A lighthouse beam sweeping out over the Atlantic from the top of a dark cliff.
column6: Roman writers put the end of the world here and believed the sun went into the sea hissing. Its light is one of the strongest in Europe.

column5: Spruce trunks going up out of frame under a star field, snow between them.
column6: With the Bavarian Forest across the German border it makes the largest unbroken stretch of forest in central Europe.

column5: Moonlit dune ridges running in parallel curves, the crests bright and the flanks black.
column6: The dunes reach about a hundred and fifty metres and move enough between years to be measured.

column5: Basalt columns stepping down into the sea, the water gone to mist in a long exposure.
column6: There are around forty thousand of them, mostly hexagons, left where a lava flow cooled and cracked.

column5: Karst peaks standing out of river mist, each one paler than the one in front.
column6: This stretch of the Li River is the landscape printed on the back of the twenty yuan note.

column5: First light on the ridges above a glen, the floor of it still dark.
column6: The glen is what is left of a supervolcano that collapsed into its own magma chamber around four hundred and twenty million years ago.

column5: A film of water on a salt flat holding the whole sky, horizon somewhere in the middle.
column6: It is the largest salt flat on earth and flat enough that satellites use it to calibrate their altimeters.

column5: The rock at last light, the desert around it already going blue.
column6: The red is iron in the surface of the sandstone that has oxidised. The colour is rust.

column5: Flooded rice terraces stepping up a mountainside, each one holding the last of the light.
column6: They were cut into the mountain by hand and are still watered from the rainforest above them.

column5: Rain coming down through moss hung branches, everything green and wet.
column6: It takes three to four metres of rain a year, and one spot inside it is marked as among the quietest places in the United States.
